claim: Parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) GABAergic interneurons mediate feedforward and feedback inhibition.
source: Parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) GABAergic interneurons mediate feedforward and feedback inhibition and have a key role in gamma oscillations and information processing.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about PV+ interneurons.

claim: PV+ interneurons have a key role in gamma oscillations and information processing.
source: Parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) GABAergic interneurons mediate feedforward and feedback inhibition and have a key role in gamma oscillations and information processing.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact.

claim: Dendritic NMDARs underlie supralinear integration of feedback excitation from local pyramidal neurons onto mouse CA1 PV+ cells.
source: Here, we show that dendritic NMDARs underlie supralinear integration of feedback excitation from local pyramidal neurons onto mouse CA1 PV+ cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 1-4.

claim: NMDARs at feedback connections onto PV+ cells enable cooperative recruitment of PV+ interneurons.
source: Furthermore, by incorporating NMDARs at feedback connections onto PV+ cells in spiking networks, we show that these receptors enable cooperative recruitment of PV+ interneurons, strengthening and stabilising principal cell assemblies.
evidence: This is demonstrated through network modeling simulations shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: NMDARs at feedback connections onto PV+ cells strengthen and stabilize principal cell assemblies.
source: Furthermore, by incorporating NMDARs at feedback connections onto PV+ cells in spiking networks, we show that these receptors enable cooperative recruitment of PV+ interneurons, strengthening and stabilising principal cell assemblies.
evidence: This is demonstrated through network modeling in Figures 5-7.

claim: Failure of NMDAR-mediated cooperative recruitment provides a parsimonious explanation for cognitive and sensory gating deficits in pathologies with impaired PV+ NMDAR signalling.
source: Failure of this phenomenon provides a parsimonious explanation for cognitive and sensory gating deficits in pathologies with impaired PV+ NMDAR signalling.
evidence: This is proposed as an interpretation of the modeling results in the context of disease pathology.

claim: PV+ cells have broad receptive fields inherited from multiple converging heterogeneously tuned principal neurons.
source: PV+ cells have broad receptive fields inherited from multiple converging heterogeneously tuned principal neurons (Kerlin et al., 2010) and coupled with their powerful somatic inhibition of principal cells, they are positioned to mediate a 'winner-takes-all' scheme in which neuronal assemblies inhibit each other (Agetsuma et al., 2018; Trouche et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PV+ cells are positioned to mediate a 'winner-takes-all' scheme in which neuronal assemblies inhibit each other.
source: PV+ cells have broad receptive fields inherited from multiple converging heterogeneously tuned principal neurons (Kerlin et al., 2010) and coupled with their powerful somatic inhibition of principal cells, they are positioned to mediate a 'winner-takes-all' scheme in which neuronal assemblies inhibit each other (Agetsuma et al., 2018; Trouche et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NMDARs contribute relatively less to synaptic excitation of PV+ cells than principal neurons.
source: Although NMDARs contribute relatively less to synaptic excitation of PV+ cells than principal neurons (Geiger et al., 1997; Lamsa et al., 2007; Matta et al., 2013), several sources of evidence suggest that they are important for the normal operation of cell assemblies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Genetic deletion of NMDARs in PV+ interneurons disrupts gamma rhythms.
source: In particular, genetic deletion of NMDARs in PV+ interneurons disrupts both gamma rhythms (Carlén et al., 2012) and spatial representations (Korotkova et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Genetic deletion of NMDARs in PV+ interneurons disrupts spatial representations.
source: In particular, genetic deletion of NMDARs in PV+ interneurons disrupts both gamma rhythms (Carlén et al., 2012) and spatial representations (Korotkova et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Impaired NMDAR-mediated signaling in PV+ interneurons has been suggested to be a core feature of schizophrenia.
source: Moreover, impaired NMDAR-mediated signaling in PV+ interneurons has been suggested to be a core feature of schizophrenia (Coyle, 2012; Lisman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Feedback synapses from local pyramidal neurons onto CA1 PV+ interneurons show NMDAR-dependent long-term potentiation.
source: A recent study investigating plasticity rules of glutamatergic inputs onto CA1 PV+ interneurons reported NMDAR-dependent long-term potentiation (LTP) at feedback synapses from local pyramidal neurons but not at feedforward connections made by Schaffer collaterals (Le Roux et al., 2013), and attributed the difference to a larger NMDAR conductance at feedback synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Feedforward connections made by Schaffer collaterals onto CA1 PV+ interneurons do not show NMDAR-dependent long-term potentiation.
source: A recent study investigating plasticity rules of glutamatergic inputs onto CA1 PV+ interneurons reported NMDAR-dependent long-term potentiation (LTP) at feedback synapses from local pyramidal neurons but not at feedforward connections made by Schaffer collaterals (Le Roux et al., 2013), and attributed the difference to a larger NMDAR conductance at feedback synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Feedback synapses have a larger NMDAR conductance than feedforward synapses onto CA1 PV+ interneurons.
source: A recent study investigating plasticity rules of glutamatergic inputs onto CA1 PV+ interneurons reported NMDAR-dependent long-term potentiation (LTP) at feedback synapses from local pyramidal neurons but not at feedforward connections made by Schaffer collaterals (Le Roux et al., 2013), and attributed the difference to a larger NMDAR conductance at feedback synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and confirmed by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Activation of uncaging locations in stratum oriens revealed supralinear uEPSP summation with peak amplitude nonlinearity of 24.0 ± 4.5%.
source: Activation of sites on dendrites in stratum oriens revealed supralinear uEPSP summation (peak amplitude nonlinearity: 24.0 ± 4.5%, mean ± SEM, n = 14; Figure 1D,E; unscaled responses in Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from glutamate uncaging experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Activation of uncaging locations in stratum oriens revealed supralinear uEPSP summation with time-integral nonlinearity of 54.0 ± 10.1%.
source: This nonlinearity was even larger when measured using the time-integral of uEPSPs measured between 0 and 50 ms from onset (time-integral nonlinearity: 54.0 ± 10.1%; Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from glutamate uncaging experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Glutamate uncaging along dendritic segments in stratum radiatum resulted in approximately linear uEPSP summation with peak amplitude nonlinearity of 3.8 ± 5.0%.
source: In contrast, when glutamate was uncaged along dendritic segments in stratum radiatum, uEPSPs summated in an approximately linear fashion (peak amplitude nonlinearity: 3.8 ± 5.0%, time-integral nonlinearity: 6.3 ± 7.6%, n = 9; oriens vs. radiatum p=0.0083 and p=0.0028 for peak amplitude and time-integral comparisons respectively, unpaired t-tests, Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from glutamate uncaging experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Glutamate uncaging along dendritic segments in stratum radiatum resulted in approximately linear uEPSP summation with time-integral nonlinearity of 6.3 ± 7.6%.
source: In contrast, when glutamate was uncaged along dendritic segments in stratum radiatum, uEPSPs summated in an approximately linear fashion (peak amplitude nonlinearity: 3.8 ± 5.0%, time-integral nonlinearity: 6.3 ± 7.6%, n = 9; oriens vs. radiatum p=0.0083 and p=0.0028 for peak amplitude and time-integral comparisons respectively, unpaired t-tests, Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from glutamate uncaging experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: The difference in integration nonlinearity between stratum oriens and stratum radiatum is statistically significant (p=0.0083 for peak amplitude, p=0.0028 for time-integral).
source: In contrast, when glutamate was uncaged along dendritic segments in stratum radiatum, uEPSPs summated in an approximately linear fashion (peak amplitude nonlinearity: 3.8 ± 5.0%, time-integral nonlinearity: 6.3 ± 7.6%, n = 9; oriens vs. radiatum p=0.0083 and p=0.0028 for peak amplitude and time-integral comparisons respectively, unpaired t-tests, Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: Feedback inputs from axon collaterals of local pyramidal cells are confined to dendrites in the stratum oriens.
source: In contrast, feedback inputs from axon collaterals of local pyramidal cells are confined to dendrites in the stratum oriens (Amaral et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: PV+ interneurons receive excitatory feedforward inputs across the full extent of their dendritic trees, in both strata radiatum and oriens.
source: Such neurons, which mainly comprise basket cells in addition to axo-axonic and bistratified cells (Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013), receive excitatory feedforward inputs across the full extent of their dendritic trees, in both strata radiatum and oriens.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Uncaging-evoked EPSPs (uEPSPs) were comparable in amplitude and kinetics to spontaneous EPSPs.
source: Activation of individual uncaging locations in either stratum evoked uncaging-evoked EPSPs (uEPSPs) that were comparable in amplitude and kinetics to spontaneous EPSPs (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with a high density of excitatory synapses innervating PV+ interneuron dendrites (Gulyás et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PV+ interneuron dendrites have a high density of excitatory synapses.
source: Activation of individual uncaging locations in either stratum evoked uncaging-evoked EPSPs (uEPSPs) that were comparable in amplitude and kinetics to spontaneous EPSPs (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with a high density of excitatory synapses innervating PV+ interneuron dendrites (Gulyás et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and consistent with experimental observations.

claim: The degree of supralinear summation was significantly lower when uncaging was distributed across two dendrites (39.3 ± 11.7%) compared to within-dendrite uncaging (16.5 ± 5.6%), p=0.016.
source: The degree of supralinear summation was significantly lower when uncaging was distributed across two dendrites (peak amplitude nonlinearity, 39.3 ± 11.7% vs 16.5 ± 5.6% for within-dendrite and across-dendrite uncaging respectively, p=0.016, n = 12; paired t-test; Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from glutamate uncaging experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The spatial clustering or dispersion of co-active dendritic inputs to PV+ interneurons has an important role in input integration.
source: This result indicates that the spatial clustering, or conversely dispersion, of co-active dendritic inputs to PV+ interneurons has an important role in input integration.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results from Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Supralinear dendritic summation in stratum oriens was abolished when NMDARs were blocked by D-AP5 (time-integral nonlinearity: 2.5 ± 3.0%, vs control p=0.0004, n = 10).
source: In line with previous evidence for a substantial NMDAR component at feedback inputs onto PV+ cells (Le Roux et al., 2013), supralinear dendritic summation in stratum oriens was abolished when NMDARs were blocked by D-AP5 (100 µM) (time-integral nonlinearity: 2.5 ± 3.0%, vs control without the drug p=0.0004, n = 10; Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Dendritic integration in stratum radiatum was unchanged by D-AP5 (time-integral nonlinearity: 3.3 ± 2.6%, vs control p=0.88, n = 4).
source: Dendritic integration in stratum radiatum was unchanged from control conditions (time-integral nonlinearity: 3.3 ± 2.6%, vs control p=0.88, n = 4; Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: TTX did not significantly affect integration in stratum oriens (time-integral nonlinearity 40.1 ± 5.6%, vs control p=0.23, n = 16).
source: In contrast to D-AP5, the sodium channel blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX, 100 nM) did not significantly affect integration in either stratum oriens or radiatum (oriens time-integral nonlinearity 40.1 ± 5.6%, vs control p=0.23, n = 16; radiatum time-integral nonlinearity 9.4 ± 3.3%, vs control p=0.71, n = 9; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: TTX did not significantly affect integration in stratum radiatum (time-integral nonlinearity 9.4 ± 3.3%, vs control p=0.71, n = 9).
source: In contrast to D-AP5, the sodium channel blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX, 100 nM) did not significantly affect integration in either stratum oriens or radiatum (oriens time-integral nonlinearity 40.1 ± 5.6%, vs control p=0.23, n = 16; radiatum time-integral nonlinearity 9.4 ± 3.3%, vs control p=0.71, n = 9; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: PV+ interneuron dendrites generally do not support regenerative events.
source: The failure of TTX to affect uEPSP integration is consistent with the view that PV+ interneuron dendrites generally do not support regenerative events (Hu et al., 2010) (although see Chiovini et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and consistent with experimental observations.

claim: Dendrites of PV+ interneurons that mediate feedback inhibition exhibit NMDAR-dependent supralinear input integration.
source: Dendrites of PV+ interneurons that mediate feedback inhibition, but not those mediating purely feedforward inhibition, thus exhibit NMDAR-dependent supralinear input integration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Clusters of coactive synapses supplied by local pyramidal neurons cooperate via depolarization-dependent relief of NMDARs from Mg2+ blockade.
source: These findings imply that clusters of coactive synapses supplied by local pyramidal neurons cooperate via depolarization-dependent relief of NMDARs from Mg2+ blockade.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Feedback inputs show a > 2 fold greater NMDAR/AMPAR charge ratio (3.5 ± 0.7) compared to feedforward inputs (1.3 ± 0.3), p=0.0017, n = 10.
source: Pharmacological dissection of EPSCs in 0.1 mM [Mg2+] revealed a > 2 fold greater NMDAR/AMPAR charge ratio when stimulating in the alveus than when stimulating in stratum radiatum (charge ratio: 3.5 ± 0.7 vs 1.3 ± 0.3, p=0.0017, n = 10, paired t-test; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from voltage clamp experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The decay time constant of NMDAR-mediated EPSCs was similar for feedforward (154.6 ± 25.9 ms) and feedback inputs (148.1 ± 13.4 ms), p=0.8, n = 10.
source: The decay time constant of the NMDAR-mediated EPSCs was similar for the two inputs (Schaffer collaterals: 154.6 ± 25.9 ms vs alveus: 148.1 ± 13.4 ms, p=0.8, n = 10, paired t-test; Figure 3B) providing no evidence for differences in NR2B subunit inclusion, again consistent with previous work that showed similar effects of selective blockade of NR2B-containing receptors (Le Roux et al., 2013) (although see Matta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from voltage clamp experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There is no evidence for differences in NR2B subunit inclusion between feedforward and feedback inputs.
source: The decay time constant of the NMDAR-mediated EPSCs was similar for the two inputs (Schaffer collaterals: 154.6 ± 25.9 ms vs alveus: 148.1 ± 13.4 ms, p=0.8, n = 10, paired t-test; Figure 3B) providing no evidence for differences in NR2B subunit inclusion, again consistent with previous work that showed similar effects of selective blockade of NR2B-containing receptors (Le Roux et al., 2013) (although see Matta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data and consistent with previous literature.

claim: Dendrites of PV+ interneurons in stratum oriens are generally thinner and shorter than those in stratum radiatum.
source: Dendrites of PV+ interneurons in stratum oriens are generally thinner and shorter than those in stratum radiatum (Gulyás et al., 1999) suggestive of a higher effective local input impedance.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Oriens dendrites may have a higher effective local input impedance than radiatum dendrites.
source: Dendrites of PV+ interneurons in stratum oriens are generally thinner and shorter than those in stratum radiatum (Gulyás et al., 1999) suggestive of a higher effective local input impedance.
evidence: This is inferred from the morphological differences cited from previous literature.

claim: Compartmental model simulations revealed supralinear summation of EPSPs that was more pronounced for stratum oriens (42.5 ± 3.5%) than stratum radiatum dendrites (23.9 ± 2.3%), p<0.001.
source: These simulations revealed supralinear summation of EPSPs recorded at the soma that was more pronounced for stratum oriens than for stratum radiatum dendrites (oriens vs radiatum time-integral nonlinearity: 42.5 ± 3.5% vs 23.9 ± 2.3%, p<0.001, Figure 3D), supporting a role for dendritic morphology in mediating the difference between strata.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from computational modeling shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Dendritic morphology has a role in mediating the difference in integration between strata.
source: These simulations revealed supralinear summation of EPSPs recorded at the soma that was more pronounced for stratum oriens than for stratum radiatum dendrites (oriens vs radiatum time-integral nonlinearity: 42.5 ± 3.5% vs 23.9 ± 2.3%, p<0.001, Figure 3D), supporting a role for dendritic morphology in mediating the difference between strata.
evidence: This is an interpretation of computational modeling results.

claim: Reducing the simulated NMDAR/AMPAR conductance ratio at radiatum dendrites to half that of oriens dendrites improved agreement with glutamate uncaging data (oriens: 42.5 ± 3.5% vs radiatum: 8.5 ± 0.8%).
source: Reducing the simulated NMDAR/AMPAR conductance ratio at radiatum dendrites to half that of the oriens dendrites, in line with results from experiments in Figure 3A, improved agreement with the glutamate uncaging data (time-integral supralinearity in simulations: 42.5 ± 3.5% vs 8.5 ± 0.8% for stratum oriens vs stratum radiatum; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from computational modeling shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The difference in dendritic integration in oriens and radiatum dendrites may be accounted for by a combination of differential NMDAR expression and dendritic morphology.
source: The difference in dendritic integration in oriens and radiatum dendrites observed experimentally (Figure 1) may therefore be accounted for by a combination of differential NMDAR expression (greater in stratum oriens) and dendritic morphology (greater impedance in stratum oriens, thus facilitating depolarization and NMDAR opening).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from combining experimental and modeling results.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of feedback fibers revealed large NMDAR currents (amplitude: 459.1 ± 89.2 pA, integral: 39.1 ± 6.8 nA ms).
source: This revealed large NMDAR currents (amplitude: 459.1 ± 89.2 pA, integral: 39.1 ± 6.8 nA ms) and NMDAR/AMPAR ratios (amplitude: 0.7 ± 0.2, integral: 2.7 ± 0.8, Figure 4C), confirming abundant expression of functional NMDARs at feedback excitatory synapses on PV+ interneurons.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of feedback fibers revealed NMDAR/AMPAR ratios of amplitude: 0.7 ± 0.2 and integral: 2.7 ± 0.8.
source: This revealed large NMDAR currents (amplitude: 459.1 ± 89.2 pA, integral: 39.1 ± 6.8 nA ms) and NMDAR/AMPAR ratios (amplitude: 0.7 ± 0.2, integral: 2.7 ± 0.8, Figure 4C), confirming abundant expression of functional NMDARs at feedback excitatory synapses on PV+ interneurons.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There is abundant expression of functional NMDARs at feedback excitatory synapses on PV+ interneurons.
source: This revealed large NMDAR currents (amplitude: 459.1 ± 89.2 pA, integral: 39.1 ± 6.8 nA ms) and NMDAR/AMPAR ratios (amplitude: 0.7 ± 0.2, integral: 2.7 ± 0.8, Figure 4C), confirming abundant expression of functional NMDARs at feedback excitatory synapses on PV+ interneurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from optogenetic experiments.

claim: Perfusion of D-AP5 significantly reduced the average time-integral of optogenetically evoked EPSPs (p=0.033, n = 5).
source: Perfusion of the NMDAR blocker D-AP5 significantly reduced both the average time-integral and the ratio of integral to peak of EPSPs evoked at the maximal light intensity (p=0.033; p=0.014; n = 5), but not the peak EPSPs (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Perfusion of D-AP5 significantly reduced the ratio of integral to peak of optogenetically evoked EPSPs (p=0.014, n = 5).
source: Perfusion of the NMDAR blocker D-AP5 significantly reduced both the average time-integral and the ratio of integral to peak of EPSPs evoked at the maximal light intensity (p=0.033; p=0.014; n = 5), but not the peak EPSPs (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: D-AP5 did not significantly affect the peak amplitude of optogenetically evoked EPSPs.
source: Perfusion of the NMDAR blocker D-AP5 significantly reduced both the average time-integral and the ratio of integral to peak of EPSPs evoked at the maximal light intensity (p=0.033; p=0.014; n = 5), but not the peak EPSPs (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: There was a larger NMDAR contribution to EPSPs elicited by stronger light pulses.
source: Furthermore, in line with cooperative postsynaptic voltage-dependent relief of Mg2+ blockade, we observed a larger NMDAR contribution to EPSPs elicited by stronger light pulses (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is an observation from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Synaptic glutamate release at feedback inputs from CA1 pyramidal cells can elicit NMDAR-mediated depolarization of PV+ interneurons.
source: Together, these experiments confirm that synaptic glutamate release at feedback inputs from CA1 pyramidal cells can elicit NMDAR-mediated depolarization of PV+ interneurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from optogenetic experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Excitatory neurons driven by a compact 'hump' of excitation in input space cooperated in recruiting NMDARs on the interneuron to a greater extent than equivalent excitation shuffled randomly in input space.
source: Excitatory neurons driven by a compact 'hump' of excitation in input space cooperated in recruiting NMDARs on the interneuron to a greater extent than equivalent excitation shuffled randomly in input space (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a result from network modeling simulations shown in Figure 5D.

claim: NMDARs on PV+ interneurons contribute to maintaining a sharp assembly representation, dependent on the spatial arrangement of active synapses on the dendritic tree.
source: We propose, therefore, that NMDARs on PV+ interneurons contribute to maintaining a sharp assembly representation, dependent on the spatial arrangement of active synapses on the dendritic tree of the interneuron.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from network modeling simulations in Figure 5.

claim: When one network received a stable and compact hump of excitation it was much more likely to 'win' than a competing network receiving an equal amount of dispersed excitation.
source: When one network received a stable and compact hump of excitation (again, with input space defined by location on the interneuron dendritic tree) it was much more likely to 'win' than a competing network receiving an equal amount of excitation that was dispersed (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a result from network modeling simulations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The tendency for the network receiving a hump of excitation to win disappeared when NMDARs were removed from the inhibitory neurons.
source: The tendency for the network receiving a hump of excitation to win disappeared when NMDARs were removed from the inhibitory neurons (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is a result from network modeling simulations shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: The frequency of flipping between competing networks increased steeply when the normalized conductance of NMDARs was decreased in the inhibitory neurons.
source: However, the frequency of flipping increased steeply when the normalized conductance of NMDARs was decreased in the inhibitory neurons, resulting in a flickering of the dominant assemblies (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a result from network modeling simulations shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The frequency of flipping was relatively unaffected by reducing the AMPAR conductance.
source: In contrast, the frequency of flipping was relatively unaffected by reducing the AMPAR conductance (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a result from network modeling simulations shown in Figure 7D.

claim: NMDAR-mediated cooperative interactions among clustered synapses on an interneuron stabilize cell assemblies.
source: We thus conclude that NMDAR-mediated cooperative interactions among clustered synapses on an interneuron stabilize cell assemblies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from network modeling simulations in Figure 7.

claim: Clustered excitatory synapses on stratum oriens dendrites of CA1 PV+ interneurons interact supralinearly.
source: The present study shows that clustered excitatory synapses on stratum oriens dendrites of CA1 PV+ interneurons interact supralinearly, challenging the view that they act as linear integrators of synaptic inputs (see also Tzilivaki et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The high impedance of stratum oriens dendrites facilitates the cooperative recruitment of NMDARs.
source: The high impedance of stratum oriens dendrites, which are innervated by axon collaterals of local pyramidal neurons, facilitates the cooperative recruitment of NMDARs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental and modeling results.

claim: An adaptive role of NMDARs in feedback excitation of PV+ interneurons is to facilitate the emergence of strong and stable cell assemblies.
source: An adaptive role of NMDARs in feedback excitation of PV+ interneurons can therefore be to facilitate the emergence of strong and stable cell assemblies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from network modeling results.

claim: Selective knockdown of NMDARs in PV+ interneurons causes working-memory deficits.
source: Selective knockdown of NMDARs in PV+ interneurons has previously been shown to cause a range of functional impairments, including working-memory deficits and a reduction in the precision of hippocampal spatial representations (Korotkova et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Selective knockdown of NMDARs in PV+ interneurons causes a reduction in the precision of hippocampal spatial representations.
source: Selective knockdown of NMDARs in PV+ interneurons has previously been shown to cause a range of functional impairments, including working-memory deficits and a reduction in the precision of hippocampal spatial representations (Korotkova et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The network simulations provide a mechanistic explanation for the reduction in spatial information conveyed by principal cell spiking observed after NMDAR knockdown in PV+ interneurons.
source: The network simulations presented here provide a mechanistic explanation for some of these results, in particular, a reduction in spatial information conveyed by principal cell spiking (Korotkova et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting modeling results to previous experimental findings.

claim: In the visual cortex PV+ inhibition increases assembly similarity.
source: Other studies highlight a role for PV+ cells and inhibition in cell-assembly competition: in the visual cortex PV+ inhibition increases assembly similarity (Agetsuma et al., 2018) and in the hippocampus silencing of a dominant assembly was shown to uncover an alternative previously inhibited assembly (Trouche et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In the hippocampus silencing of a dominant assembly uncovered an alternative previously inhibited assembly.
source: Other studies highlight a role for PV+ cells and inhibition in cell-assembly competition: in the visual cortex PV+ inhibition increases assembly similarity (Agetsuma et al., 2018) and in the hippocampus silencing of a dominant assembly was shown to uncover an alternative previously inhibited assembly (Trouche et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: NMDARs may be integral to PV+ cell functions in cell-assembly competition.
source: The present study indicates that NMDARs may be integral to these functions.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current study's findings to previous literature.

claim: NMDAR blockers recapitulate some features of schizophrenia in healthy individuals.
source: For instance, NMDAR blockers have been shown to recapitulate some features of schizophrenia in healthy individuals (Krystal et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: NMDAR antagonists cause a net disinhibition of principal cell activity.
source: When coupled with the observation that NMDAR antagonists cause a net disinhibition of principal cell activity (Homayoun and Moghaddam, 2007; Jackson et al., 2004), it has been suggested that cortical circuits are especially vulnerable to failure of NMDAR-mediated signaling in PV+ interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Post-mortem studies have revealed a selective loss of PV+ interneurons in people with schizophrenia.
source: Moreover, post-mortem studies have revealed a selective loss of PV+ interneurons in people with schizophrenia (Lewis et al., 2012) and overexpression of Neuregulin 1, a leading schizophrenia susceptibility gene, is associated with a reduction of NMDARs on PV+ cells (Kotzadimitriou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Overexpression of Neuregulin 1 is associated with a reduction of NMDARs on PV+ cells.
source: Moreover, post-mortem studies have revealed a selective loss of PV+ interneurons in people with schizophrenia (Lewis et al., 2012) and overexpression of Neuregulin 1, a leading schizophrenia susceptibility gene, is associated with a reduction of NMDARs on PV+ cells (Kotzadimitriou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Destabilization of dominant neuronal assemblies resulting from impaired NMDAR signaling on PV+ interneurons may explain a failure of sensory gating in schizophrenia.
source: Destabilization of dominant neuronal assemblies, as shown here to result from impaired NMDAR signaling on PV+ interneurons, may thus explain a failure of sensory gating (Javitt and Freedman, 2015) and evidence for reduced cognitive control, for instance in the Necker cube test (McBain et al., 2011), in schizophrenia.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current study's findings to schizophrenia pathophysiology.

claim: Destabilization of dominant neuronal assemblies resulting from impaired NMDAR signaling on PV+ interneurons may explain reduced cognitive control in schizophrenia.
source: Destabilization of dominant neuronal assemblies, as shown here to result from impaired NMDAR signaling on PV+ interneurons, may thus explain a failure of sensory gating (Javitt and Freedman, 2015) and evidence for reduced cognitive control, for instance in the Necker cube test (McBain et al., 2011), in schizophrenia.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current study's findings to schizophrenia pathophysiology.

claim: Recurrent connections between PV+ interneurons and local pyramidal cell circuits are found throughout the brain.
source: Recurrent connections between PV+ interneurons and local pyramidal cell circuits are found throughout the brain.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about brain anatomy.

claim: Experiments were performed in acute hippocampal slices from mice obtained by crossing PV-Cre mice with Ai9 mice.
source: Experiments were performed in acute hippocampal slices from mice obtained by crossing PV-Cre mice with Ai9 mice, and tdTomato expression was used to target fast-spiking PV+ interneurons in CA1 stratum pyramidale.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: PV+ interneurons in CA1 stratum pyramidale mainly comprise basket cells in addition to axo-axonic and bistratified cells.
source: Such neurons, which mainly comprise basket cells in addition to axo-axonic and bistratified cells (Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013), receive excitatory feedforward inputs across the full extent of their dendritic trees, in both strata radiatum and oriens.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Wide-field illumination pulses of 470 nm light elicited monophasic EPSCs in PV+ interneurons.
source: Wide-field illumination pulses (1 ms) of 470 nm light elicited monophasic EPSCs, in agreement with the low associative connectivity among CA1 pyramidal neurons (Amaral et al., 1991; Deuchars and Thomson, 1996) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CA1 pyramidal neurons have low associative connectivity.
source: Wide-field illumination pulses (1 ms) of 470 nm light elicited monophasic EPSCs, in agreement with the low associative connectivity among CA1 pyramidal neurons (Amaral et al., 1991; Deuchars and Thomson, 1996) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and consistent with experimental observations.
